title: Relative Hopf kernel shear isomorphisms and their naturality
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. A commutative Hopf $k$-algebra here means a unital commutative $k$-algebra $A$ with $k$-algebra maps $\Delta_A:A\to A\otimes_k A$, $\epsilon_A:A\to k$, $S_A:A\to A$ such that $(\Delta_A\otimes1)\Delta_A=(1\otimes\Delta_A)\Delta_A$, $(\epsilon_A\otimes1)\Delta_A=(1\otimes\epsilon_A)\Delta_A=1_A$, and $\mu_A(S_A\otimes1)\Delta_A=\mu_A(1\otimes S_A)\Delta_A=\eta_A\epsilon_A$, under the usual tensor unit and associativity identifications; $\mu_A$ and $\eta_A$ are multiplication and unit. Tensor products are those of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. A Hopf homomorphism $u:P\to Q$ means a $k$-algebra homomorphism with $\Delta_Qu=(u\otimes u)\Delta_P$, $\epsilon_Qu=\epsilon_P$ and $S_Qu=uS_P$. Let $C,A,B$ be commutative Hopf $k$-algebras and let $u:C\to A$, $i:A\to B$ be Hopf homomorphisms. Put $C^+=\ker\epsilon_C$, $D=A/(u(C^+)A)$ and $E=B/((iu)(C^+)B)$ [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. These quotients have the induced commutative Hopf $k$-algebra structures, and $i$ induces a Hopf homomorphism $\alpha:D\to E$, $\bar a\mapsto\overline{i(a)}$. There are $B$-algebra isomorphisms, with $B$ acting through the second tensor factor,
$$\Phi_A:A\otimes_C B\xrightarrow{\sim}D\otimes_k B,\qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto\sum\bar a_{(1)}\otimes i(a_{(2)})b,$$
$$\Phi_B:B\otimes_C B\xrightarrow{\sim}E\otimes_k B,\qquad x\otimes b\longmapsto\sum\bar x_{(1)}\otimes x_{(2)}b.$$
Here $B$ is a $C$-algebra through $iu$, $\Delta_A(a)=\sum a_{(1)}\otimes a_{(2)}$ and $\Delta_B(x)=\sum x_{(1)}\otimes x_{(2)}$ are finite tensor presentations. Their inverses are
$$\bar a\otimes b\longmapsto\sum a_{(1)}\otimes i(S_A(a_{(2)}))b,\qquad\bar x\otimes b\longmapsto\sum x_{(1)}\otimes S_B(x_{(2)})b,$$
independently of the lifts $a,x$. With $a_i=i\otimes_C1_B$ and $b_i=\alpha\otimes_k1_B$, one has $\Phi_Ba_i=b_i\Phi_A$. No injectivity, flatness, finite-type, or surjectivity hypothesis is imposed on $u$ or $i$.

source.place: Exercises 2-1 and 2-2, printed pp.61--62, and the two diagrams in Theorem 3.31, p.74: the explicit coordinate maps of the kernel/product trivializations; Proposition 3.12, p.67, for quotient Hopf structures.

proof.text: Work simultaneously with $(X,v,h)=(A,u,i)$ and $(B,iu,1_B)$; thus $hv=iu$. Write $I=v(C^+)X$, $Q=X/I$, and $q:X\to Q$. For $c\in C$, $c-\epsilon_C(c)1\in C^+$, so $qv(c)=\epsilon_C(c)1$. Applying $\epsilon_C$ to $\sum c_{(1)}S_C(c_{(2)})=\epsilon_C(c)1$ and then using the counit identity gives $\epsilon_CS_C(c)=\epsilon_C(c)$. Consequently the three algebra maps $(q\otimes q)\Delta_X$, $\epsilon_X$, and $qS_X$ vanish on every $v(c)$ with $c\in C^+$: their respective values on $v(c)$ are $\epsilon_C(c)(1\otimes1)$, $\epsilon_C(c)$, and $\epsilon_C(S_C(c))1$. Since these maps are multiplicative and additive they vanish on $I$.

source.place: Proposition 3.12, p.67, quotient construction expanded on the generators of the ideal; Definition 3.3, pp.65--66.

proof.text: Define $\Delta_Q(qx)=(q\otimes q)\Delta_X(x)$, $\epsilon_Q(qx)=\epsilon_X(x)$ and $S_Q(qx)=qS_X(x)$. Step 1 proves independence of the representative: changing $x$ by an element of $I$ changes each value by zero. These are unital algebra maps because their composites with the surjective algebra map $q$ are. Coassociativity on $qx$ is the image of coassociativity on $x$ under $q\otimes q\otimes q$; the two counit equations on $qx$ are the images under $q$ of the counit equations on $x$. Likewise the two antipode products on $qx$ are $q(\sum S_X(x_{(1)})x_{(2)})$ and $q(\sum x_{(1)}S_X(x_{(2)}))$, both $\epsilon_X(x)1_Q$. Every element is $qx$, proving all the Hopf axioms and that $q$ preserves the structure maps.

source.place: Proposition 3.12, p.67, routine verification written out; Definition 3.3, pp.65--66.

proof.text: The map $i$ carries each generator $u(c)$ of $u(C^+)A$ to the generator $iu(c)$ of $(iu)(C^+)B$, and hence carries the first ideal into the second. Define $\alpha(q_Aa)=q_Bi(a)$; differences of representatives map to zero, so this is a well-defined unital $k$-algebra homomorphism. On $q_Aa$ its comultiplication identity is $(q_B\otimes q_B)\Delta_Bi(a)=(q_Bi\otimes q_Bi)\Delta_A(a)$; its counit and antipode identities follow respectively from $\epsilon_Bi=\epsilon_A$ and $S_Bi=iS_A$. Surjectivity of $q_A$ proves that $\alpha$ is Hopf.

source.place: Proposition 3.12, p.67, factorization on quotient representatives; Theorem 3.31, p.74, lower horizontal map.

proof.text:
For either triple of step 1, put $F=(q\otimes h)\Delta_X:X\to Q\otimes_kB$. This is a $k$-algebra map. For $c\in C$, the Hopf property of $v$ and the equation $qv=\eta_Q\epsilon_C$ give
$$F(v(c))=\sum\epsilon_C(c_{(1)})1\otimes hv(c_{(2)})=1\otimes iu(c).$$
Thus $F$ and $b\mapsto1\otimes b$ agree on $C$. Equip $Q\otimes_kB$ with this common $C$-algebra structure and apply the tensor universal property to obtain the algebra map
$$\Phi_X:X\otimes_CB\to Q\otimes_kB,\qquad x\otimes b\mapsto\sum q(x_{(1)})\otimes h(x_{(2)})b.$$
It is a $B$-algebra map because $\Phi_X(1\otimes b)=1\otimes b$.

source.place: Exercises 2-1 and 2-2, pp.61--62; coordinate form of the vertical isomorphisms in Theorem 3.31, p.74.

proof.text:
Define the $k$-algebra map $T:X\to X\otimes_CB$ by $T(x)=\sum x_{(1)}\otimes hS_X(x_{(2)})$. It is the composite of $\Delta_X$ with the tensor map induced by $x\mapsto x\otimes1$ and $x\mapsto1\otimes hS_X(x)$; commutativity ensures these are algebra maps with commuting images. Balancing over $C$ and the antipode equation give
$$T(v(c))=\sum v(c_{(1)})\otimes hvS_C(c_{(2)})=1\otimes hv\!\left(\sum c_{(1)}S_C(c_{(2)})\right)=\epsilon_C(c)(1\otimes1).$$
Thus $T$ kills the generators of $I$ and, being an algebra map, kills $I$. The rule $\bar T(qx)=T(x)$ is independent of the lift and is an algebra map on $Q$. Apply the tensor universal property over $k$ to $\bar T$ and $b\mapsto1\otimes b$. This gives a $B$-algebra map $\Psi_X:Q\otimes_kB\to X\otimes_CB$ with $\Psi_X(qx\otimes b)=\sum x_{(1)}\otimes hS_X(x_{(2)})b$.

source.place: Exercises 2-1 and 2-2, pp.61--62, inverse division map; Definition 3.3, pp.65--66, antipode equations.

proof.text:
Coassociativity, followed by the two antipode equations and the counit equation, computes the two composites:
$$\Psi_X\Phi_X(x\otimes b)=\sum x_{(1)}\otimes h(S_X(x_{(2)})x_{(3)})b=x\otimes b,$$
$$\Phi_X\Psi_X(qx\otimes b)=\sum q(x_{(1)})\otimes h(x_{(2)}S_X(x_{(3)}))b=qx\otimes b.$$
For example the first sum is $(1\otimes h)\bigl(\sum x_{(1)}\otimes S_X(x_{(2)})x_{(3)}\bigr)(1\otimes b)$, and the parenthesis is $\sum x_{(1)}\otimes\epsilon_X(x_{(2)})1=x\otimes1$; the second uses the other antipode identity in exactly the displayed order. Pure tensors generate the tensor products additively, and every element of $Q$ lifts along $q$, so the two identities hold everywhere. Hence $\Phi_X$ and $\Psi_X$ are inverse $B$-algebra isomorphisms.

source.place: Exercises 2-1 and 2-2, pp.61--62, multiplication/division cancellation expressed by Definition 3.3, pp.65--66.

proof.text:
Specializing $(X,v,h)$ to $(A,u,i)$ and $(B,iu,1_B)$ gives precisely the two asserted isomorphisms and their lift-independent inverses. The tensor universal property defines $a_i=i\otimes_C1_B$ and $b_i=\alpha\otimes_k1_B$. On $a\otimes b$ their composites with the shears agree, since
$$\Phi_Ba_i(a\otimes b)=\sum q_B(i(a_{(1)}))\otimes i(a_{(2)})b=\sum\alpha(q_A(a_{(1)}))\otimes i(a_{(2)})b=b_i\Phi_A(a\otimes b).$$
Here the first equality is exactly $\Delta_Bi=(i\otimes i)\Delta_A$, and the second is the defining equation of $\alpha$. Additivity gives equality on the whole tensor product. Every construction used only the stated Hopf equations and tensor balancing, so requires none of the excluded additional hypotheses.

source.place: Theorem 3.31, p.74, compatibility of its two vertical kernel/product isomorphisms, expanded on coordinates.
